title: Nostalgia
description: Four radio extracts about nostalgia: an essay, an interview with a psychologist, a talk on its uses and a listener call-in.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A radio essay
parts.intro: You will hear the opening of a radio essay about nostalgia.

script.speaker: Elena
script.text: The word nostalgia was coined by a young Swiss doctor in the late seventeenth century, and he did not mean it kindly. He used it to describe a condition afflicting soldiers who were far from home, a longing so intense that it brought on fever, fainting and, in some cases, death. For two centuries afterwards, nostalgia was treated as a disease, something to be cured with leeches, opium or, rather more sensibly, a trip back to the mountains.

script.speaker: Elena
script.text: How strange, then, that we now use the word so lightly. We speak of nostalgia for a favourite cartoon, a flavour of sweet or a certain kind of summer afternoon. Somewhere along the way, the ache lost its sting, and what remained was a gentle, faintly sugared sadness. The pain turned into pleasure, or at least into something we are content to pay for.

script.speaker: Elena
script.text: And yet it is worth asking what we are actually longing for. I used to believe that I missed my childhood home. But when I visited it again last spring, I found a small, rather shabby house, and I felt nothing at all. It dawned on me that what I missed was not the place but the person I was when I lived there: unhurried, protected and certain that the best was still to come.

script.speaker: Elena
script.text: That is the paradox at the heart of the feeling. Nostalgia seems to point backwards, but it is really a comment on the present. We are rarely wistful when we are content. The past that we long for has been quietly edited, with the boredom and the humiliations removed, until it resembles a place that never quite existed.

script.speaker: Elena
script.text: I do not think that makes the feeling worthless. A fiction can still console. But I have come to suspect that the pull of the past tells us less about history than about what we feel is missing now.

parts.title: Part 2 · An interview with a psychologist
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Daniel, interviewing a psychologist, Dr Fraser.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Dr Fraser, the old doctors thought nostalgia was a sickness. What does the research say?

script.speaker: Dr Fraser
script.text: Quite the opposite, in fact. Studies over the last twenty years suggest that nostalgia is, on balance, good for you. When people are asked to recall a cherished memory, their mood tends to lift, they feel more connected to others and they report a stronger sense that life has meaning.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That seems counterintuitive. Surely dwelling on the past makes the present feel worse?

script.speaker: Dr Fraser
script.text: That's what many people assume, and sometimes it does. But the typical nostalgic memory is not a lonely one. It usually features other people, a family meal, a friend, a team. So the feeling acts a bit like a reminder that you are loved, and that reminder is especially useful when you're feeling isolated or low.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: So it's a coping mechanism.

script.speaker: Dr Fraser
script.text: In part. In one experiment, people who were made to feel lonely were more inclined to feel nostalgic afterwards, as though the mind reaches for a remedy. And they became more optimistic about forming new friendships, which is the opposite of retreating into the past.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Is there a downside?

script.speaker: Dr Fraser
script.text: Certainly. If nostalgia becomes a refuge from every difficulty, then it can keep someone from engaging with life as it is. People who grieve, for example, can become stuck. The sensible view is that it's a tool. Used in moderation, it nourishes. Used as a hiding place, it can starve you.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: And does it change with age?

script.speaker: Dr Fraser
script.text: Interestingly, it doesn't disappear when you're young. Teenagers feel it too, often about early childhood, and the feeling seems to peak during periods of transition, such as leaving school or moving to a new city.

parts.title: Part 3 · A talk on nostalgia and society
parts.intro: You will hear a cultural historian discussing how nostalgia is used in business and politics.

script.speaker: Professor Hale
script.text: Nostalgia is a private feeling, but it has never remained private for long. Those who sell things have always understood its power. A familiar tune, a retro package or a revived television series can persuade us to open our wallets precisely because it makes us feel safe. When the future looks uncertain, the past becomes a very profitable product.

script.speaker: Professor Hale
script.text: Politics has learned the same lesson. A slogan that promises to restore former greatness is almost always more effective than one that promises uncertain change, because it asks people to recover something they already believe they had. The trouble, of course, is that the golden age being invoked is usually an invention. It leaves out the people who suffered in it.

script.speaker: Professor Hale
script.text: Historians distinguish between two kinds of longing. Restorative nostalgia insists that the past was real and can be rebuilt, which is the type that leads to rigid and sometimes dangerous movements. Reflective nostalgia, by contrast, accepts that the past is gone, and lingers over the ache with irony and affection. The first wants to go home. The second knows that it cannot.

script.speaker: Professor Hale
script.text: I'd argue that this second kind is the more humane. It allows us to cherish what we lost without demanding that anyone else pay for the restoration. And it often generates art, because the gap between what was and what is happens to be where poems and songs live.

script.speaker: Professor Hale
script.text: So I am not an enemy of nostalgia. I am simply suspicious of anyone who offers to sell it to me, whether in a shop or at a rally.

parts.title: Part 4 · Listeners call in
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Mai, speaking on air with a listener, Tom.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: We have Tom on the line, who says he has a story about nostalgia. Tom, you're on air.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Hello, Mai. Yes, I'll try to be brief. I recently cleared out my late father's workshop. It was a cluttered shed full of jars of screws and half-finished projects, and honestly, it smelled of oil and sawdust. I assumed I'd be miserable, but I found I couldn't stop smiling.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: What was it that made you smile?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: It was the smell, mostly. It took me straight back to being seven years old, sitting on an upturned bucket while he fixed my bicycle. I could hear the radio he always had on, tuned to a station that played old songs. I suddenly realised that I hadn't thought of those afternoons for decades.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: So you were surprised by how happy it made you.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Very. I'd expected grief. What I got was gratitude, and it was a warm sort of gratitude. I ended up keeping only a few things, a battered spirit level and a tin of nails. I didn't want to turn the shed into a museum.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: That sounds a very healthy approach. Do you feel you've lost him all over again by clearing it?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Not at all, which surprised me too. I think I realised that he isn't in the objects. I carry him around with me, especially when I'm fixing something badly in my own kitchen. I'd just like to say that if anyone is putting off a job like this, it may turn out kinder than you expect.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Thank you, Tom. That's a lovely note to end on, and a reminder that the past can be visited without being rebuilt.

questions.text: What was nostalgia originally understood to be?
options: A gentle pleasure enjoyed by soldiers on leave
A talent for remembering home in great detail
A fear of travel affecting young doctors
A disease afflicting soldiers far from home
questions.explanation: The word was coined for a condition in soldiers far from home, causing fever and fainting.

evidence.quote: a condition afflicting soldiers who were far from home

questions.text: What does Elena mean by saying the ache lost its sting?
options: The disease was finally cured by doctors
The feeling became gentler and more pleasant
The feeling disappeared once people stopped suffering
People stopped using the word altogether
questions.explanation: She says the pain turned into a gentle, sugared sadness, even a pleasure.

evidence.quote: the ache lost its sting

questions.text: What did Elena realise on visiting her childhood home?
options: She missed who she was then, not the place
She felt sad about the neighbours who had left
The house was much improved since she last saw it
She wanted to buy it back and move in
questions.explanation: She says she missed the person she was when she lived there.

evidence.quote: what I missed was not the place but the person I was when I lived there

questions.text: What is Elena's view about the past we long for?
options: It was always unhappy and full of humiliations
It has been edited and tidied in memory
It was exactly as we remember it now
It cannot be discussed without sadness
questions.explanation: She says the past has been quietly edited, with boredom and humiliation removed.

evidence.quote: The past that we long for has been quietly edited

questions.text: What does she conclude about nostalgia?
options: It reveals what we feel is missing in the present
It should be avoided because it makes people unhappy and passive
It is a form of illness, as the doctors thought
It teaches us accurate history about the past
questions.explanation: She suspects the pull of the past tells us less about history than about what we feel is missing now.

evidence.quote: what we feel is missing now

questions.text: What does recent research say about nostalgia?
options: It has no real effect on mood
It is generally harmful to wellbeing
It affects only the elderly
It is generally beneficial to people
questions.explanation: Studies suggest it is, on balance, good for you.

evidence.quote: nostalgia is, on balance, good for you

questions.text: Why does Dr Fraser say nostalgic memories tend to be helpful?
options: They usually involve other people
They concern the distant past of childhood
They concern successes achieved at work
They are always rather brief
questions.explanation: The typical nostalgic memory features other people and reminds you that you are loved.

evidence.quote: It usually features other people

questions.text: What happened to people made to feel lonely in the experiment?
options: They avoided other people for several days afterwards
They became angry with their closest friends
They became more optimistic about new friendships
They lost all interest in the past altogether
questions.explanation: They felt nostalgic and grew more optimistic about forming friendships.

evidence.quote: more optimistic about forming new friendships

questions.text: What is Dr Fraser's view of nostalgia as a refuge?
options: It is harmful if it replaces engaging with life
It is always the best response to difficulty
It is harmless in every case, however used
It only affects people who are grieving
questions.explanation: She says used as a hiding place it can starve you.

evidence.quote: Used as a hiding place, it can starve you.

questions.text: What does Dr Fraser say about age?
options: Only older people feel it, usually in retirement
Teenagers feel it too, often during transitions
It peaks in middle age, once children leave
It disappears with time as memories fade
questions.explanation: She says teenagers feel it too and it peaks in periods of transition.

evidence.quote: the feeling seems to peak during periods of transition

questions.text: Why does the speaker say the past is a profitable product?
options: Uncertainty makes people seek safety in familiar things
Shops sell old objects at higher prices
People forget what things used to cost
Old products are cheaper to produce than new ones
questions.explanation: When the future looks uncertain, the past makes us feel safe and we spend money.

evidence.quote: it makes us feel safe

questions.text: What is his criticism of political nostalgia?
options: It is always sincere, so voters trust it
The golden age it invokes is usually an invention
It appeals only to people who suffered then
It is too expensive to maintain for long
questions.explanation: He says the golden age is usually an invention that leaves out those who suffered.

evidence.quote: the golden age being invoked is usually an invention

questions.text: How does reflective nostalgia differ from restorative nostalgia?
options: It insists that the past can be rebuilt
It rejects art and poetry as sentimental
It accepts that the past is gone
It leads to rigid and dangerous movements
questions.explanation: Reflective nostalgia accepts the past is gone and lingers over the ache with irony.

evidence.quote: accepts that the past is gone

questions.text: Why does he say the gap between past and present is important?
options: It is where shops compete for customers
It is where much art is created
It is where history comes to an end
It is where political slogans begin
questions.explanation: He says it is where poems and songs live.

evidence.quote: where poems and songs live

questions.text: What is his final position?
options: He loves every kind of nostalgia equally
He hates nostalgia in all its forms
He is suspicious of those who sell nostalgia
He ignores nostalgia as a harmless fashion
questions.explanation: He says he is not an enemy of nostalgia but suspicious of anyone who sells it.

evidence.quote: I am simply suspicious of anyone who offers to sell it to me

questions.text: What did Tom do recently?
options: Retired from work after more than forty years
Cleared out his late father's workshop
Bought a new bicycle for his own children
Sold his father's old shed to a neighbour
questions.explanation: He says he cleared out his late father's workshop.

evidence.quote: I recently cleared out my late father's workshop

questions.text: What triggered Tom's memory?
options: The smell of oil and sawdust
An old bicycle left in the shed
A song on his father's radio
A photograph of his father
questions.explanation: He says it was the smell, mostly, that took him back to being seven.

evidence.quote: It was the smell, mostly.

questions.text: How did Tom feel contrary to his expectation?
options: Angry and resentful rather than sentimental
Embarrassed rather than proud of him
Bored and restless rather than curious
Grateful rather than grief-stricken
questions.explanation: He expected grief but got a warm gratitude.

evidence.quote: What I got was gratitude

options: He did not want to make the shed a museum
His family wanted to keep most of the things
They were the only valuable items in the shed
He had no space for them in his own home
questions.explanation: He says he didn't want to turn the shed into a museum.

evidence.quote: I didn't want to turn the shed into a museum.

questions.text: What message does Tom give to other listeners?
options: Never throw away your family's belongings
Sell old tools as quickly as you can
Avoid your family's belongings until you feel ready
Such a task may be kinder than expected
questions.explanation: He says if anyone is putting off a job like this, it may be kinder than expected.

evidence.quote: it may turn out kinder than you expect
